summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for managing RADIUS authentication servers. It replaces RFC 2619 by deprecating the table limited to IPv4 addresses and adding a new one using version-neutral IP addresses, and adds UNITS and REFERENCE clauses to some objects.

plainLanguage.summary: A RADIUS server is the system that decides whether a user or device may join a network. This RFC defines the SNMP counters such a server keeps about itself and about each client it talks to, and updates them so the client addresses can be IPv4 or IPv6.

subtitle: The SNMP counters a RADIUS authentication server keeps about itself and each client, redone so they work with IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The RADIUS Authentication Server MIB of RFC 2619 could only hold IPv4 addresses, so a server that also handled IPv6 clients had no standard way to report them or to keep per-client counters for them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC deprecates the IPv4-only radiusAuthClientTable and adds radiusAuthClientExtTable, whose address columns use the version-neutral InetAddress types. The remaining objects from RFC 2619 are carried forward, and UNITS and REFERENCE clauses are added to selected objects.
tldr.outcome: One set of client tables and counters now covers both IP versions, and a deprecated table may still be kept for older management stations. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2619.

today: RFC 4669 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2619, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
The memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. The objects defined relate to the Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Authentication Server as defined in RFC 2865.

Section 2 fixes one piece of vocabulary. The document uses the word malformed with respect to RADIUS packets, particularly in the context of counters of malformed packets. While RFC 2865 does not provide an explicit definition of malformed, it generally means that the implementation has determined the packet does not match the format defined in RFC 2865. Some implementations may determine that packets are malformed when the Vendor Specific Attribute format does not follow the RFC 2865 recommendations for VSAs; those implementations are used in deployments today, and thus set the de facto definition of malformed.

Section 3 places the module in the Internet-Standard Management Framework, pointing readers to Section 7 of RFC 3410 for a detailed overview. Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the MIB, and are generally accessed through SNMP. The memo specifies a MIB module compliant to SMIv2, described in STD 58, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: A RADIUS server is the system that decides whether a user or device may join a network. This RFC defines the SNMP counters such a server keeps about itself and about each client it talks to, and updates them so the client addresses can be IPv4 or IPv6.

sections.title: Scope of the Changes
sections.content:
The document obsoletes RFC 2619, the RADIUS Authentication Server MIB, by deprecating the radiusAuthClientTable and adding a new table, radiusAuthClientExtTable, containing radiusAuthClientInetAddressType and radiusAuthClientInetAddress. The purpose of the added objects is to support version-neutral IP addressing formats, and the existing table containing radiusAuthClientAddress is deprecated. The remaining MIB objects from RFC 2619 are carried forward into this document, and the memo also adds UNITS and REFERENCE clauses to selected objects.

The RFC quotes the recommendation of RFC 4001, which defines the SMI textual conventions for version-neutral IP addresses, and which this memo follows. The recommendation reads: in particular, when revising a MIB module that contains IPv4 specific tables, it is suggested to define new tables using the textual conventions defined in that memo that support all versions of IP. The status of the new tables SHOULD be current, whereas the status of the old IP version specific tables SHOULD be changed to deprecated. The other approach, of having multiple similar tables for different IP versions, is strongly discouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is a rewrite rather than an addition. The table that listed clients held IPv4 addresses only, so it is marked as deprecated and a new table takes its place, with address fields that can hold either kind of address. The rest of the objects are carried over unchanged, apart from extra units and reference notes.

sections.title: The Structure of the Module
sections.content:
The RADIUS authentication protocol described in RFC 2865 distinguishes between the client function and the server function. In RADIUS authentication, clients send Access-Requests and servers reply with Access-Accepts, Access-Rejects and Access-Challenges. Typically, NAS devices implement the client function and would be expected to implement the RADIUS authentication client MIB, while RADIUS authentication servers implement the server function and would be expected to implement this server MIB.

It is possible for a RADIUS authentication entity to perform both functions. A RADIUS proxy, for example, may act as a server to one or more RADIUS authentication clients while simultaneously acting as an authentication client to one or more authentication servers. In such situations it is expected that RADIUS entities combining client and server functionality will support both the client and server MIBs. The server MIB is defined in this document and the client MIB in RFC 4668.

The MIB module contains fourteen scalars as well as a single table, the RADIUS Authentication Client Table, which contains one row for each RADIUS authentication client with which the server shares a secret. Each entry in that table includes thirteen columns presenting a view of the activity of the RADIUS authentication server. The module imports from RFC 2578, RFC 2580, RFC 3411 and RFC 4001.

The module is named RADIUS-AUTH-SERVER-MIB. Its root radiusAuthServMIB sits under radiusAuthentication, which sits under radiusMIB, and that in turn is at mib-2 67. The radiusMIB object is described as the OID assigned to RADIUS MIB work by IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS has two sides. A client is the device asking for a decision, usually a router or switch; a server is the system that makes it. This MIB is for the server side, though a proxy that does both jobs is expected to implement both MIBs. The module keeps a set of counters for the server as a whole, plus a table with a row for each client the server shares a secret with.

sections.title: The Deprecated Table and When to Keep It
sections.content:
The deprecated table in this MIB is carried forward from RFC 2619. There are two conditions under which it MAY be desirable for managed entities to continue to support it.

  1. The managed entity only supports IPv4 address formats.
  2. The managed entity supports both IPv4 and IPv6 address formats, and the deprecated table is supported for backwards compatibility with older management stations. The RFC says this option SHOULD only be used when the IP addresses in the new table are in IPv4 format and can accurately be represented in both the new table and the deprecated table.

Managed entities SHOULD NOT instantiate row entries in the deprecated table, which contains IPv4-only address objects, when the RADIUS client address represented in such a table row is not an IPv4 address. They SHOULD NOT return inaccurate values of IP address or SNMP object access errors for IPv4-only address objects in otherwise populated tables.

The RFC also gives a rule for correlating the two tables: when row entries exist in both the deprecated IPv4-only table and the new IP-version-neutral table that describe the same RADIUS client, the row indexes SHOULD be the same for the corresponding rows in each table, to facilitate correlation of these related rows by management applications.
sections.plainLanguage: An old table that only understands IPv4 addresses is kept in the MIB, but marked as deprecated. A server may keep filling it in if it only deals in IPv4, or if older management tools still expect to read it. When both tables describe the same client, they should use the same row number so a tool can match them up.

sections.title: The Counters
sections.content:
The new table radiusAuthClientExtTable is described as the conceptual table listing the RADIUS authentication clients with which the server shares a secret, with one row for each such client. Its index is radiusAuthClientExtIndex, an Integer32 in the range 1 to 2147483647 that uniquely identifies each client the server communicates with.

The address columns are radiusAuthClientInetAddressType, of type InetAddressType, which gives the type of address format used, and radiusAuthClientInetAddress, of type InetAddress, which gives the IP address of the client using the version-neutral address format. radiusAuthClientExtID is the NAS-Identifier of the client, with a reference to Section 5.32 of RFC 2865, and the RFC notes that this is not necessarily the same as sysName in MIB II.

Each row then carries nine counters, all of type Counter32 with the unit packets: radiusAuthServExtAccessRequests, radiusAuthServExtDupAccessRequests, radiusAuthServExtAccessAccepts, radiusAuthServExtAccessRejects, radiusAuthServExtAccessChallenges, radiusAuthServExtMalformedAccessRequests, radiusAuthServExtBadAuthenticators, radiusAuthServExtPacketsDropped and radiusAuthServExtUnknownTypes. The row also holds radiusAuthServCounterDiscontinuity, a TimeTicks marking when the counters last jumped.

The module states the arithmetic that ties them together. Responses equal AccessAccepts plus AccessRejects plus AccessChallenges. And Requests minus DupRequests, BadAuthenticators, MalformedRequests, UnknownTypes and PacketsDropped equals the number of entries logged.

The same ten counters also exist at the server level, with a Total prefix: radiusAuthServTotalAccessRequests, radiusAuthServTotalInvalidRequests, radiusAuthServTotalDupAccessRequests, radiusAuthServTotalAccessAccepts, radiusAuthServTotalAccessRejects, radiusAuthServTotalAccessChallenges, radiusAuthServTotalMalformedAccessRequests, radiusAuthServTotalBadAuthenticators, radiusAuthServTotalPacketsDropped and radiusAuthServTotalUnknownTypes. The descriptions give the meaning: the number of packets received on the authentication port, the number of Access-Request packets received from unknown addresses, and the number of RADIUS packets of unknown type that were received, among others.

Four more scalars describe the server itself. radiusAuthServIdent is an implementation identification string for the RADIUS authentication server software in use, for example 'FNS-2.1'. radiusAuthServUpTime is the time elapsed in hundredths of a second since the server process was started, and is zero for software without persistent state. radiusAuthServResetTime is the time elapsed since the server was reset, and is zero for software with no persistence or no reset operation. radiusAuthServConfigReset is a status and action object with the values other(1), reset(2), initializing(3) and running(4); when set to reset(2) the persistent server state is reinitialized as if the server had just been started, and that value is never returned by a read.
sections.plainLanguage: The server-wide counters count the packets it has received: requests, duplicates, accepts, rejects, challenges, malformed packets, bad authenticators, dropped packets and packets of an unknown type. The table repeats the same counters for each individual client, so you can see which client is misbehaving. The counts can jump when the server restarts, and a timestamp records when that last happened.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that a number of management objects have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and that support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. There is one such object. radiusAuthServConfigReset can be used to reinitialize the persistent state of any server: when set to reset(2), the persistent server state is reinitialized as if the server had just been started. Depending on the server implementation details this action may or may not interrupt the processing of pending requests in the server, and the RFC says abuse of this object may lead to a denial of service attack on the server.

There are also objects that may contain sensitive information. radiusAuthClientIPAddress and radiusAuthClientInetAddress can be used to determine the address of the RADIUS authentication client with which the server is communicating, and that information could be useful in mounting an attack on the authentication client. The RFC says it is thus important to control even GET access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP, and that not all versions of SNMP provide features for such a secure environment.

The RFC then repeats the usual position on SNMP versions: those prior to SNMPv3 do not provide a secure environment, and even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is no control over who on the secure network may read or change the objects in this MIB. It recommends that implementers consider the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for the SNMPv3 cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of earlier versions is not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: One object can restart the server, so a person who can write it can cause a denial of service. The table also reveals the addresses of the clients talking to the server, which is useful to an attacker, so reading it should be controlled too. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its authentication and privacy features.

items.title: AccessRequests
items.text: Packets received on the authentication port.

items.title: AccessRejects and AccessChallenges
items.text: The two reply types that refuse or query a client, alongside the accepts.

items.title: MalformedAccessRequests
items.text: Requests that did not match the format in RFC 2865.

items.title: BadAuthenticators
items.text: Requests whose authenticator did not match.

items.title: UnknownTypes and Discontinuity
items.text: RADIUS packets of an unknown type, and when the counters last jumped, usually after a restart.
